content: Non-oliguric hyperkalemia in newborns is defined as a plasma potassium concentration exceeding 6.5 mmol/L, occurring without evidence of acute renal failure. This condition is frequently observed within the first 48 hours of life in very low birth weight (VLBW) infants (birth weight < 1500 g) and/or those born very prematurely (< 32 weeks of gestation). The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of various interventions for managing non-oliguric hyperkalemia in preterm or VLBW neonates during their first 72 hours of life. For the purposes of this review, non-oliguric hyperkalemia was defined as a serum potassium level greater than 6.0 mmol/L (a threshold at which clinical interventions are typically initiated) and a urine output exceeding 0.5 mL/kg/hour. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, with the initial search conducted in 2006 and an update performed in 2011. The review focused on randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving preterm and/or VLBW neonates diagnosed with non-oliguric hyperkalemia. Interventions studied included those aimed at redistributing serum potassium (e.g., sodium bicarbonate, insulin and glucose), enhancing potassium elimination (e.g., diuretics, ion exchange resins, exchange transfusion, peritoneal dialysis, salbutamol, or albuterol), or mitigating the risk of hyperkalemia-induced arrhythmias (e.g., calcium). Comparisons were made against placebo, no intervention, or between different interventions. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality during the initial hospital stay, while secondary outcomes included common adverse events in preterm infants. Three randomized trials involving a total of 74 preterm infants (with outcome data available for 71 infants) were included in the review. Urine output was reported in only one study (Hu 1999). None of the trials ensured adequate concealment of group allocation, and the sample sizes were small, with 12 infants in one study (Malone 1991), 19 in another (Singh 2002), and 40 in the third (Hu 1999). Blinding of clinical staff to the intervention and outcome assessments was not achieved in two of the studies (Malone 1991; Hu 1999). In the study by Malone (1991), the combination of insulin and glucose was compared to treatment with a cation-exchange resin. The insulin and glucose intervention resulted in a reduction in all-cause mortality, which approached statistical significance (relative risk [RR] 0.18, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.03 to 1.15; risk difference [RD] -0.66, 95% CI -1.09 to -0.22; number needed to treat to benefit [NNTB] 2, 95% CI 1 to 5). In the study by Hu (1999), the incidence of intraventricular hemorrhage (grade 2 or higher) was significantly reduced with the intervention (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.93; RD -0.35, 95% CI -0.62 to -0.08; NNTB 3, 95% CI 2 to 13). In the study by Singh (2002), albuterol inhalation was compared to saline inhalation. Albuterol significantly reduced serum potassium levels at four hours (weighted mean difference [WMD] -0.69 mmol/L, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.51) and eight hours (WMD -0.59 mmol/L, 95% CI -0.78 to -0.40) after treatment initiation. However, no differences were observed in mortality or other clinical outcomes. No serious adverse effects were reported with either the insulin and glucose combination or albuterol inhalation. Other interventions, such as diuretics, exchange transfusion, peritoneal dialysis, and calcium, have not been evaluated in randomized controlled trials. The authors concluded that due to the limited data from small and methodologically weak studies, no definitive clinical recommendations can be made. However, the combination of insulin and glucose appears to be more effective than rectal cation-exchange resin for treating hyperkalemia in preterm infants. Both the insulin and glucose combination and albuterol inhalation warrant further investigation, potentially in direct comparison with each other. Other interventions for non-oliguric hyperkalemia remain untested in randomized controlled trials.
